summary.summary: Rother's 2023/24 treasury outturn shows cash running down fast: investments halved from £29.8m at Q3 to £14.5m at 31 March 2024 as the council paused borrowing and funded capital spending from its own balances, leaving it £17.9m under-borrowed against a £49.6m capital financing requirement with external debt steady at £31.7m. Interest income of £1.427m beat the £586k budget and the overall treasury surplus was £841k. The watch items are concentration rather than compliance: a £4.6m loan at 9% to its wholly-owned housing company with a further £41.5m of company borrowing/lending programmed for 2024/25, £8m in pooled property funds now worth £922,707 less than cost (shielded by the IFRS9 statutory override until March 2025), and a £32.8m commercial property portfolio. All borrowing stayed comfortably within the £192.8m authorised limit.

signals.headline: £4.6m loan at 9% to Rother DC Housing Company, with a further £41.5m of company borrowing/loan programmed for 2024/25 and £26.3m for 2027/28
signals.why: The planned lending to a single subsidiary is more than double the council's entire current £31.7m debt, concentrating credit risk in one company.

signals.headline: Treasury investments halved to £14.5m by 31 March 2024 (from £29.8m at Q3), with £8m locked in property funds and part of the balance owed to precepting bodies
signals.why: Liquid cash is thin against £31.7m debt and Q3 had already flagged possible short-term borrowing for cash purposes (none was ultimately needed).

signals.headline: Q4-revised capital programme shows £25.2m of general borrowing plus £41.5m housing-company borrowing/loan in 2024/25, against £31.7m current debt — programme still under affordability review
signals.why: If delivered as tabled, Rother's debt would roughly triple in one year at post-2022 interest rates.

compliance.notes: Scored from a complete pack: the cover report plus all three appendices, including the Treasury Management Strategy that had been published 'TO FOLLOW'. No document is missing, so no caveat applies. HRA: judged NOT to have one - 'HRA' and 'Housing Revenue Account' appear nowhere in the 53 pages, no CFR or financing-cost indicator carries a GF/HRA split, and housing delivery runs entirely through the wholly owned RDC Housing Company financed by General Fund capital loans, so LB-04 is marked not applicable and the HRA limbs of PI-02, PI-07 and GOV-07 do not arise. Strongest areas are the liability benchmark (charted to 2075 with all four balances and genuine commentary on the gap), the counterparty and creditworthiness policy, and the CFR reconciliation. The three material weaknesses are the complete absence of any maturity-structure indicator for borrowing (PI-09, core - the treasury indicator section sets only the authorised limit and operational boundary, and the table numbering runs 1-15 unbroken so nothing has been omitted from the copies supplied), the absence of fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02, core), and the 2026/27 suite reaching Cabinet only on 11 May 2026 - over five weeks after the financial year began - so the strategy, indicators and MRP statement were approved after the year had started, contrary to the pack's own statement at App2 s30 (RPT-01). Also noted: Table 10 projects gross debt above the CFR from 2027/28 without comment; App1 s5.4 quotes CFR figures that do not agree with App2 Table 3; and the Capital Strategy's cross-references to 'Appendix B' tables in fact point to tables inside Appendix 2, which is a labelling slip rather than a missing document.

gaps.evidence: App2 p.4 s22: the CFR includes long-term liabilities such as PFI and finance leases but 'The Council currently does not have any such arrangements'; App1 p.16 s11.3 covers finance-lease borrowing costs; App3 p.13 lists a S151 duty to give members a schedule of investments including financial guarantees
App1 p.4 s4.12 states compliance with paragraph 51 of the Prudential Code
App1 p.4 s4.11 contingency plans 'include disposing of assets and restructuring debt arrangements'; App1 p.17 s11.6-11.8 disposals and the Asset Disposal Policy adopted November 2024

App3 p.7 s25 'Investment Risk Benchmarking': 'The Council will use an investment benchmark to performance of its cash deposit investments with a maturity date of up to one year'; App3 p.6 s6 monitors yield against appropriate benchmarks

App3 pp.8-10 Appendix D classifies money market funds (CNAV, LVNAV, VNAV), ultra-short dated bond funds and property funds, noting property funds 'can be deemed to be capital expenditure'; App3 p.2 s5(l) covers the IFRS 9 statutory override for pooled investments to 31.3.29; App3 p.7 s27-30 external fund managers

news_drafts.headline: Auditors warn of financial pressure at Rother as reserves deplete and housing company loan nears
news_drafts.lead: Rother Council faces financial pressure over the coming years, auditors have warned. The council's reserves, a financial cushion for unexpected costs, are forecast to fall from £2.5 million to £1.2 million by 2028/29—a 52 per cent cut. More pressing is the £35.6 million loan to the council's housing company, which must be repaid by March 2028. Repayment depends on completion and sale of 200 homes; only three had been completed by July 2026 and none sold. The company posted losses of £2.1 million in 2025/26. The council's spending cuts delivered only 44 per cent of their target in 2025/26, compared with 87 per cent the previous year, forcing draws on its reserves. The 2026/27 budget was approved in balance without using reserves—an improvement—but auditors issued two new recommendations on financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Only two of seven prior-year audit recommendations have been fully addressed; five remain partially implemented or in progress
findings.detail: Auditors reviewed progress on seven recommendations made in previous year audits. Two have been fully addressed or no longer require action; the remaining five have only been partially addressed or remain ongoing.
findings.matters: Slow implementation of audit recommendations indicates that identified governance and financial management weaknesses are persisting rather than being resolved
findings.figures: 2 of 7 fully addressed; 5 of 7 partially addressed or in progress
findings.quote: 2 of the 7 recommendations have been addressed or do not require any further action, with five recommendations partially addressed or in progress.

findings.headline: Auditors identified two new improvement recommendations specifically for Financial Sustainability
findings.detail: Following assessment of the Council's value for money arrangements, Grant Thornton has issued two new recommendations for improvement in Financial Sustainability. The detailed recommendations are set out in the auditor's full annual report.
findings.matters: Improvement recommendations indicate specific areas where the Council's financial management and planning require strengthening according to external auditors
findings.quote: This year only two new improvement recommendations have been identified, these are outlined on page 36 of the appendix

findings.headline: Auditors raised specific concerns about the Council's available reserves and the financial position of Rother DC Housing Company Ltd
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's audit report specifically flagged concerns about the adequacy of the Council's available reserves and the financial position of Rother DC Housing Company Ltd, noting that the housing company's financial difficulties are directly affecting the Council's overall financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy and subsidiary company financial health are fundamental measures of financial sustainability that lenders assess when deciding whether to lend to a council
findings.quote: The Committee should note the External Auditor's concerns regarding the financial resilience of the Council, in particular regarding its available reserves, the financial position of Rother DC Housing Company Ltd and its related impact upon the Council's own financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery improved to 98% in 2025/26, up from 83%, and emerging cost pressures are being escalated to members promptly.
findings.detail: Capital delivery improved materially to 98% (£42m of £43m) in 2025/26 from 83% the prior year. The auditor notes that emerging cost pressures (e.g. Sidley Depot project increasing from £1.1m to £2.2m) are identified and reported to members, and project governance is 'catching and managing risk before it becomes a wider problem'. This contrasts with operational budget slippage.
findings.matters: Strong capital delivery and governance signals the council can execute projects and manage risk when requirements are clear and fixed (capital) rather than when dependent on income forecasts or external factors (revenue savings). This is a positive counterweight to savings delivery failures.
findings.figures: Capital delivery 98% (£42m of £43m) in 2025/26, up from 83% in 2024/25
findings.quote: capital delivery improving to 98% (£42m of £43m) during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is scheduled for April 2028 but government has announced a pause to review the programme, creating planning uncertainty.
findings.detail: Government confirmed in July 2026 that Rother would move to a single East Sussex unitary authority from 1 April 2028, with the 'One East Sussex' business case modelling £64m cumulative savings by 2032/33. However, government announced in September 2026 a pause in LGR decisions pending review of legal advice and wider devolution priorities, creating uncertainty about timeline and scope. The council notes this creates 'further uncertainty into this timetable' and has suspended 'detailed term financial and service planning until the government's position is clarified'.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on whether and when the council's corporate structure changes. A merger creates transition risks (loss of senior staff, dual running costs, disrupted service delivery) and the auditor notes the RDCHC business plan has been delayed pending LGR decisions, meaning the council cannot finalise its medium-term plan. Extended uncertainty is costly.
findings.figures: Proposed vesting date 1 April 2028; 'One East Sussex' modelling £64m cumulative savings by 2032/33
findings.quote: Government confirmed in July 2026 that Rother District Council will move to a single East Sussex unitary authority, under the 'One East Sussex' business case modelling cumulative savings of £64m by 2032/33, with vesting day of the new unitary authority 1 April 2028. East Sussex and Brighton form part of the cohort of LGR areas subject to a pause pending further [details pending clarification]
